sayIt: It's just a one-five-six-four in G the whole way through.

example.caption: C, G, Am, F: the chords behind hundreds of pop songs.

sayIt: There's a two-five-one into C at the end of the bridge.

example.caption: Dm, G, C: the strongest way to land on the home chord.

sayIt: Let's warm up with a twelve-bar in A.

example.caption: The first line: four bars of the one chord, then the four chord.

meaning: A number on its own means the chord built on that note of the key. In G, "the four" is C and "the five" is D. "The six minor" is the minor chord on the 6th note: Em in G.
whyItMatters: Bands talk in numbers so the same instructions work in any key. If you know the key, you can turn "go to the four" into a chord straight away.
sayIt: Stay on the one for the intro, then go to the four when the vocals come in.

example.caption: In G: the one (G), the four (C), the five (D), back to the one.

meaning: A song built from just the one, four and five chords of a key.
whyItMatters: Thousands of rock, folk, country and church songs use only these three chords. Know them in a key and you can follow a huge number of songs by ear.
sayIt: Don't worry, it's a three-chord trick: one, four, five.

example.caption: C, F, G, C: the one, four and five in C.

meaning: The chords of a song, in order. Each chord is "a change" because it is where the harmony changes.
whyItMatters: When someone asks "do you know the changes?" they are asking whether you know the chords, not the melody.
sayIt: Send me the changes and I'll learn it before Saturday.

example.caption: The changes of a simple song in C: C, Am, F, G.

meaning: A short run of chords at the end of a section that leads back to its start, often 1-6-2-5.
whyItMatters: The turnaround tells everyone the section is about to repeat. Hearing it coming means you are never caught out by the next "one".
sayIt: Play the turnaround twice, then we go into the second verse.

example.caption: C, Am, Dm, G, then back home to C.

meaning: To move from a chord that sounds tense to one that sounds settled, usually from the five chord to the one.
whyItMatters: Endings, choruses and turnarounds are all built on this pull. Knowing which chord wants to resolve tells you where the song is heading.
sayIt: Hold the five for a bar before you resolve; let them wait for it.

example.caption: G7 pulls hard towards C. Hear the tension, then the relief.

meaning: A quick chord played on the way between two others, to make the move smoother.
whyItMatters: Passing chords are why a song can sound fancier than its chord chart. If you hear an extra chord you cannot place, it is often one of these.
sayIt: Throw a passing chord in between the one and the two.

example.caption: C, then C♯dim for a moment, then Dm: the bass climbs by half steps.

meaning: A bass line that moves one step at a time between two chords, while the chords above it change little.
whyItMatters: Walk-downs are the stepping bass you hear under ballads and gospel. They also make jumping between chords easier, because the left hand only moves one key at a time.
sayIt: Do the walk-down from the one to the four going into the chorus.

example.caption: C, C/B, Am, Am/G, F: the lowest note steps down C, B, A, G, F.

meaning: One note held or repeated in the bass while the chords above it change. Not the sustain pedal under your foot.
whyItMatters: A pedal builds tension and is very easy for your left hand: it stays on one key while the right hand moves.
sayIt: Keep a C pedal in the left hand under the whole intro.

example.caption: C stays in the bass while the chords above move.

sayIt: It's all power chords in the verse, so keep the keys simple.

example.caption: C5, F5, G5: root and 5th, plus the root an octave up.

meaning: Play the suspended (sus4) version of a chord first, then let the 4th fall to the 3rd for the normal chord.
whyItMatters: Sus-to-major moves are a favourite in worship, pop and film music. They add a little tension and release without changing the chord.
sayIt: On the last chord, sus it and then resolve.

example.caption: Gsus4 then G: the C drops to B.

meaning: The opening of a song before the singing starts. Often it is the chorus chords, or a riff.
whyItMatters: The intro sets the key and speed for everyone, including the singer, so it needs to be steady and clear.
sayIt: Four bars of intro on the one, then the verse.

example.caption: A simple intro in C: the one and the four, twice.

meaning: The part of a song that tells the story. The music repeats each time, but the words change.
whyItMatters: Verses are usually quieter and simpler than the chorus, so play less here and save energy for later.
sayIt: Keep it soft in the first verse, just the left hand.

example.caption: A typical verse in C: C, Am, F, G.

meaning: A short section between the verse and the chorus that builds up to the chorus.
whyItMatters: It often ends on the five chord, which makes the chorus feel like an arrival. Play a little louder each bar.
sayIt: Build through the pre-chorus and stop dead on the last beat.

example.caption: F, G, Am, then a long G that leans into the chorus.

meaning: The part of a song that comes back with the same words and music each time. Usually the catchiest and loudest part.
whyItMatters: Everyone knows the chorus, so it is the part to learn first. Its chords often start on the four or the one.
sayIt: Double the last chorus and end on the one.

example.caption: A chorus in C that starts on the four: F, C, G, Am.

meaning: A section that comes once, usually after the second chorus, with chords and a melody not heard before.
whyItMatters: The bridge gives the ear a break before the last chorus. It often starts on a chord the song has not leaned on yet, such as the six minor or the four.
sayIt: Let's take it from the bridge.

example.caption: A bridge in C that starts on Am: Am, F, C, G.

meaning: The closing part of a song, after the last chorus.
whyItMatters: Endings are where bands fall apart. Agree how it ends: a fade, a repeat of the chorus, or one last chord together.
sayIt: For the outro, repeat the last line three times and hold the one.

example.caption: F, G, then a long C to finish.

meaning: Repeat the last line of the song, usually two or three times, before the ending.
whyItMatters: A tag is called on the spot, so watch the leader and keep cycling the last few chords until the final one.
sayIt: Tag the last line twice, I'll nod on the final time.

example.caption: The last line, F, G, C, played again before the end.

meaning: Repeat a short chord pattern, often two chords, over and over until someone cues the next part.
whyItMatters: Vamps fill time during a speech, a solo or a long intro. Keep it steady and keep your eyes on whoever will cue the change.
sayIt: Vamp on the one and the four until the singer's ready.

example.caption: C and F, back and forth.

meaning: Start the song again from the very beginning.
whyItMatters: It is the most common call in rehearsal. Go back to the intro chord and wait for the count in.
sayIt: Nearly. Let's take it from the top.

example.caption: Back to the first chord of the intro: C.

meaning: A section where most of the band stops or plays very quietly, leaving one or two instruments.
whyItMatters: If the keys are left alone in a breakdown, simple held chords sound best. Play less, not more.
sayIt: Break it down to just keys and voice for the last chorus.

example.caption: Soft, long chords: Am, F, C, G.

meaning: Your turn to make up a melody over the chords while the rest of the band keeps playing them.
whyItMatters: The notes of the key's scale always fit, and the chord's own notes fit best. The jam-along shows you both while you try.
sayIt: Take a solo over the verse chords, sixteen bars.

example.caption: A short idea using notes of C major over C and F.

sayIt: It's in G, starts on the one.

example.caption: In G, the song feels at home on G.

sayIt: That's too high for me; can we take it down to A?

example.caption: 1-5-6-4 in C, then the same numbers in A.

meaning: Move the song into a new key part way through. "Up a tone" means up a whole step, so C becomes D and every chord moves up two half steps.
whyItMatters: Last choruses often go up a tone to lift the energy. Use the numbers: the chords keep the same numbers, only the key changes.
sayIt: We modulate up a tone for the last chorus, so C goes to D.

example.caption: C, F, G in C, then A leads into the same chords in D: D, G, A.

meaning: A key change where everything moves up one half step: C becomes D♭. Often done suddenly between choruses.
whyItMatters: It is the most dramatic key change in pop. Your hand shape stays the same; every key just moves one to the right.
sayIt: Last chorus goes up a half step, straight in, no warning.

example.caption: C, F, G in C, then D♭, G♭, A♭ a half step up.

sayIt: The bridge drops to the relative minor.

example.caption: C major, then its relative minor, A minor: same notes, sadder home.

meaning: A clamp a guitarist puts across the strings to raise everything they play. "Capo 2" means their chords sound two half steps (a tone) higher than the shapes they hold.
whyItMatters: A guitarist with a capo often calls chords by their shapes, not by what sounds. If they say "G, capo 2", the real chord is A, so play A.
sayIt: I'm playing G shapes with a capo on 2.

example.caption: G (the shape the guitarist holds), then A (what you hear with capo 2).

meaning: The "one, two, three, four" someone calls before the band starts, at the speed of the song.
whyItMatters: The count-in sets the speed. You come in on the "one" right after it, all together.
sayIt: I'll count it in: one, two, one-two-three-four.

example.caption: Four beats counted, then everyone comes in on the next one.

meaning: The first beat of each bar, where the music feels strongest. Chord changes almost always land on it.
whyItMatters: If you know where the one is, you know when to change chord. Count "1, 2, 3, 4" and move on the 1.
sayIt: Everybody hits the last chord on the one.

example.caption: Chords that change on each one: C, then G, then Am, then F.

meaning: A bass drum on every beat: boom, boom, boom, boom. The beat of disco and dance music.
whyItMatters: It is very steady, so it is the easiest beat to lock into. Short chords on the off beats (between the booms) sound great over it.
sayIt: Go four on the floor for the last chorus.

example.caption: Short chords between the kicks, Am to F.

meaning: The drums play as if the song were half as fast (the snare on beat 3 instead of 2 and 4), while the chords keep the same speed.
whyItMatters: Half time makes a section feel bigger and heavier without slowing down. Hold your chords longer to match it.
sayIt: Drop to half time in the bridge, then back to the full beat.

example.caption: Long, heavy chords: Am, F, C, G.

meaning: A bouncy feel where each beat is split long-short ("da-ba, da-ba") instead of evenly.
whyItMatters: Blues and a lot of old rock and roll are played with a shuffle. If straight notes sound stiff, the song is probably swung.
sayIt: It's a shuffle; think long-short.

example.caption: The one and four of a blues in A.

meaning: Playing steadily, right in time with the drums and bass, so the band sounds like one machine.
whyItMatters: Being in the pocket matters more than playing lots of notes. A simple part right on the beat beats a busy part that drifts.
sayIt: Keys, sit in the pocket with the bass; don't rush.

example.caption: One chord a bar, steady: C, Am, F, G.

meaning: Short, loud chords the whole band plays together at the same moment.
whyItMatters: Hits only work if everyone lands together, so count carefully and lift your hands straight after.
sayIt: There are three hits before the chorus: F, G, C, then silence.

example.caption: Three short hits: F, G, C.

meaning: Playing the chords in a rhythm to back up a singer or soloist, without playing the tune.
whyItMatters: Most of a keyboard player's time in a band is comping. Leave space for the singer and keep the rhythm steady.
sayIt: Just comp behind me on the verses, I'll take the melody.

example.caption: Chords on the beats, not the melody: C, Am, F, G.

meaning: A short burst of notes in a gap, usually at the end of a phrase or section, before the next one starts.
whyItMatters: Fills keep a song moving between lines. One short fill where the singer breathes beats ten that get in the way.
sayIt: Give me a little fill going into the chorus.

example.caption: Hold C, then a quick run G, A, B into the next C.

meaning: A short pattern of notes that repeats through a song and is part of what makes it recognisable.
whyItMatters: Learn the riff first and the song falls into place, because it often outlines the chords.
sayIt: Bass and keys double the riff in the intro.

example.caption: A riff that walks up through the C chord and back.

meaning: Play the same notes, but 12 keys higher (or lower), where they sound brighter (or deeper).
whyItMatters: Moving a part up an octave keeps it out of the way of the bass and the singer without changing any notes.
sayIt: Take that line up an octave; you're clashing with the guitar.

example.caption: C, E, G low, then the same up an octave.

meaning: Hold the last chord and let it sound until the leader cuts everyone off together.
whyItMatters: Endings sound tidy when everyone stops at the same moment. Watch the leader's hand, not your keys.
sayIt: Let the last chord ring and watch me for the cut.

example.caption: G, then C held to the end.
